title: Specialising enough to be findable
description: Why 'I help businesses use AI' gets silence and 'I automate claims intake for regional P&C insurance brokers' gets replies — and how to find the version of that sentence that's true for you.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a niche narrow enough to be memorable from one too broad to mean anything
Evaluate a positioning statement against what a specific buyer would recognise as their problem

contentSections.body:
Two LinkedIn bios, posted the same week. One says: "I help businesses leverage AI to work smarter." Forty-one people view the profile. Zero reply to the connection note.

The other says: "I automate claims intake for regional P&C insurance brokers — the OCR-to-adjuster handoff, not the whole company." Nineteen views. Four replies, one of them a broker who'd been trying to hire someone for this exact thing for three months and didn't know the job title to search for.

contentSections.scenario:
Three consultants describe what they do:

**A:** "I help small businesses use AI to save time and grow."

**B:** "I automate return-authorization emails for Shopify stores doing $2-10M in DTC apparel."

**C:** "I build custom GPT wrapper apps for the vegan cheese subscription box industry."
contentSections.question: Which one is positioned to actually get hired?

options.label: A — broadest reach, most potential clients
B — specific process, specific vertical, real buyer
C — most specific of all, so most differentiated

feedback.a: "Save time and grow" is what every consultant of every kind claims. A buyer scanning a hundred profiles like this has no way to tell you apart from the other ninety-nine, and no way to know if you've ever touched their actual problem.
feedback.b: Right size. "Return-authorization emails" is a process a DTC ops person recognises instantly, and the revenue band tells them whether you're in their budget before they even message you. Narrow enough to be memorable, broad enough that the category — DTC apparel doing $2-10M — actually contains hundreds of companies.
feedback.c: This niche is real, but it's sized for maybe eleven companies on earth. You will run out of prospects before you run out of runway. Specificity is not the goal by itself — specificity that still points at a market with enough buyers in it is the goal.

contentSections.concept: **A findable niche has two coordinates: a process narrow enough to name, and a market wide enough to feed you.** Most people who fail at positioning err toward A — too broad to be memorable. The failure mode nobody warns you about is C: narrow enough to feel bold, narrow enough that there's no one left to sell to.

contentSections.body:
The process axis matters more than the industry axis, and it's the one people skip. "AI consultant for law firms" still describes forty different jobs — contract review, billing automation, intake triage, e-discovery, client-facing chatbots. A managing partner reading that has no idea which one you do, so they read it as none of them.

"I cut contract-review time for boutique M&A firms by pre-flagging the clauses their associates spend the first two hours hunting for" describes one job. It's longer, and it converts better, because the reader doesn't have to do any translation work to know if it's them.
Name the process, not just the industry. "AI for law firms" is forty jobs; a buyer needs to recognise theirs.

contentSections.title: Finding your version of the sentence

contentSections.body: You don't invent a niche from nothing. You look at the work you've actually already done — the automations you built, the processes you understand well enough to have opinions about, the industries where you have even one contact — and you write down where those three circles overlap.

contentSections.scenario: You've built: an invoice-coding pipeline for a property management client (Airtable + Make + Claude for line-item classification), a returns-triage bot for a friend's candle DTC brand (Zapier + GPT for routing), and a scheduling assistant for a solo dentist (n8n + calendar API). You have no other industry contacts.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually strengthens a first positioning statement right now?

items.label: The invoice-coding pipeline for property management
The returns-triage bot for the candle brand
"Healthcare AI" — dentistry is technically healthcare, and it's a bigger, higher-budget market
"AI automation for small business" — covers all three so nothing is left out

explanation.invoice: Real, built, defensible — you can talk about the actual line-item edge cases you hit. This is evidence, not a claim.
explanation.returns: Same reasoning. A second real build in a second vertical is a legitimate second option, not a distraction — see the worked example next for how to choose between them rather than claim both.
explanation.healthcare: One dental client is not evidence for "healthcare." Healthcare procurement, compliance and budget cycles for a hospital system share almost nothing with a solo dentist's calendar. Reaching for the bigger label on the strength of one small, unrelated engagement is the fastest way to sound credible to nobody, including the dentist's own peers, who will ask a question you can't answer.
explanation.generalist: Covering all three by naming none of them specifically is exactly the mistake from the first pod — it reads as "I've done a bit of everything," which a buyer correctly parses as "not yet good at any one thing."

contentSections.synthesis: Pick the strongest single overlap and lead with it. You can mention the others as range once someone's already talking to you — but the sentence that gets the reply names one thing.

contentSections.body: If you're choosing between the invoice pipeline and the returns bot, choose by market size and repeat-buyer potential, not by which one felt more impressive to build. Property management is a large, fragmented market with a recognisable budget line for this kind of work; a single candle brand is one company, not a market. "Invoice coding for property management companies" can be said to a thousand prospects. "Returns automation for the exact kind of candle company my friend runs" can be said to maybe thirty, and you'd be starting most conversations from zero rather than from a genuine sample of one.
Your niche isn't invented — it's the strongest overlap between what you've actually built and a market big enough to keep feeding you.

title: Where these clients actually look
description: A property manager doesn't search 'AI consultant.' They search 'AppFolio invoice reconciliation' or ask in a Facebook group for property managers. Positioning only works pointed at where your buyer already is.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which channels a specific vertical buyer actually uses to solve this kind of problem
Rule out channels that feel productive but structurally can't reach this buyer

contentSections.title: Your buyer isn't searching your words

contentSections.body: You post "Now offering AI automation consulting" on a general freelancer marketplace. Six months and forty proposals later: two small jobs, both underpriced, both won on price against twelve other bidders. Meanwhile a consultant you know got their first three retained clients from a single comment in a property management Facebook group, replying to someone complaining about manually re-keying invoices every Friday.

contentSections.scenario: The marketplace has huge traffic — thousands of buyers post jobs there every week. The Facebook group has 4,000 members. Both are technically "where buyers are." One produced almost nothing; the other produced a client.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that made the difference?

options.label: The marketplace is oversaturated with cheap overseas competition; the group has none
The group members had already self-selected into your exact vertical and were already discussing the exact pain, unprompted
Facebook is simply a better platform than marketplaces

feedback.saturation: Real and part of it — marketplaces do compress you into a price race with the cheapest bidder on earth. But saturation alone doesn't explain why the group worked; a saturated market with no relevant buyers in it would still fail.
feedback.self_select: This is it. Every person in that group is a property manager, by definition, and the person complaining about re-keying invoices had already diagnosed their own pain in public, unprompted. You weren't pitching a stranger a problem they might have — you were answering a question that had already been asked.
feedback.platform: Facebook isn't magic — a general Facebook feed with no vertical grouping would perform like the marketplace. It's the *self-selected, vertical-specific group*, not the platform brand.

contentSections.mechanism: **Reach a buyer where they've already grouped themselves by the problem, not where the most people are.** A channel's total size is close to irrelevant; what matters is whether everyone in it already shares the specific pain your niche solves. General platforms dilute you back into the generalist pool you spent lesson one narrowing out of.

contentSections.body:
Concretely, for most AI-automation niches, four channel types outperform general marketplaces:

- **Vertical software communities** — the Slack/Discord/forum built around the tool your buyer already runs (an AppFolio or Buildium user group for property managers, a QuickBooks ProAdvisor community for bookkeepers).
- **Trade associations and their events** — smaller, less glamorous than an AI conference, and full of people who already have the budget line and the pain.
- **Adjacent vendors and their partner programs** — the software company your buyer already pays often has a partner directory for implementation help. Getting listed there is one email.
- **Warm referral, engineered rather than hoped for** — every finished engagement, ask directly: "who else do you know running the same process the same painful way?" This is the highest-converting channel of all four and the one people forget to actually ask for.
Find the room your buyer already sorted themselves into by the pain, not the room with the most people in it.

Not every channel that reaches your buyer is worth the hours. A booth at a regional trade show might reach forty exactly-right buyers for $3,000 and a lost weekend; a well-aimed comment in a Slack thread might reach five for free and twenty minutes.

contentSections.scenario: A solo consultant tracked their own first-year client acquisition across every channel they tried. They spent roughly equal effort across a general AI-consulting directory listing, a vertical Slack community, warm referral asks after each project, and cold email to a purchased list.
contentSections.question: What share of that consultant's paying clients in year one came from warm referral asks, alone?
contentSections.explanation: 55%, in this real pattern — and it's a common one, not an outlier. Referral is the channel most people treat as a bonus rather than a system, and it's usually the one doing most of the work, because a referred lead arrives already trusting you and already sold on the problem being solvable. The directory listing and the purchased cold list, combined, produced one client, at a lower price than anything else. That's not a reason to skip cold outreach entirely — lesson three covers making it work — but it explains why referral asks belong in every single project close-out, not as an afterthought.

contentSections.body: This doesn't mean cold outreach or content don't work — module three's writing lesson exists because they can. It means: before spending a Tuesday on a channel, ask honestly whether the people in it are already grouped by the exact pain you solve, and whether you're spending real hours or borrowed ones. A bad-day version of business development is a five-minute referral ask sent from bed after a finished project. A trade-show booth is not.
Rank channels by how pre-selected the audience already is for your exact pain, not by raw reach — and put a real referral ask into every project close-out.

title: Writing that explains your offer
description: The outreach message, the one-pager, the case-study post — the writing that has to do the convincing before anyone agrees to spend thirty minutes talking to you.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a structure for outreach that names the problem before the offer
Produce a rewrite of weak outreach that would get a reply

contentSections.body:
"Hi! I'm an AI automation consultant helping businesses like yours save time with cutting-edge technology. Would love to hop on a quick call to discuss how I can help you leverage AI! Let me know what works for your calendar."

This message has been sent, in some near-identical form, to nearly every small business owner with a LinkedIn profile. It gets ignored at a rate that would be a crisis metric in any other part of the business.

contentSections.code:
Subject: AI Automation for [Company Name]

Hi [First Name],

I help businesses like yours leverage AI to save time and
cut costs. Would love to hop on a quick 15-minute call to
show you what's possible.

Best,
[Name]
contentSections.question: This gets almost no replies. What's the single biggest reason?

options.label: It should offer a bigger discount to get attention
It asks for a call before proving it understands the reader's actual problem
The subject line needs an emoji to stand out in the inbox

feedback.discount: Price isn't the blocker here — the reader hasn't even understood what they'd be buying yet. Discounting an unclear offer just makes an unclear offer cheaper.
feedback.call_first: Right. "Businesses like yours" and "what's possible" tell the reader nothing about their specific situation. Asking for fifteen minutes before demonstrating you understand their process specifically is asking them to do the work of figuring out if this is relevant — and most won't bother.
feedback.emoji: A louder subject line on a message with nothing specific inside it just gets a faster, more annoyed delete.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The template is generic in exactly the places it needs to be specific: the problem, the mechanism, and the proof. A reader can't tell if you've ever seen their business or copy-pasted this to four hundred people — because you did. The fix isn't more enthusiasm, it's naming their process by name.

contentSections.problem: Rewrite that outreach message for a real target: a regional property management company running AppFolio, with 40+ units, where you've noticed (from a public review or job posting) that they're hiring an 'accounts receivable coordinator' — a signal the AR process is manual and painful.

steps.label: Name the specific problem, not the category
steps.work: "I noticed you're hiring an AR coordinator — usually a sign the invoice-matching and delinquency-notice process in AppFolio is still manual."
steps.why: This is one sentence and it proves you looked at their actual situation. A generic message can't do this because it wasn't written for them.

steps.label: State the mechanism in one sentence, no jargon
steps.work: "I build a pipeline that matches AppFolio invoices against bank deposits automatically and flags exceptions for a human — most property managers I've worked with cut that reconciliation from a full day a week to under an hour."
steps.why: One number, one concrete before/after. Not 'leverage AI' — the actual mechanism, named plainly enough that a non-technical reader understands it on first read.

steps.label: Make the ask small and specific
steps.work: "Would it be useful to see a two-minute walkthrough of how it handles a messy AppFolio export? No call needed — I can just send the video."
steps.why: A 15-minute call is a real cost to a busy operator who doesn't know you yet. A two-minute async video is a much smaller yes, and it's the actual proof, not a promise of proof later.

steps.label: Sign off without pressure
steps.work: "No pressure either way — happy to just leave this here if the timing's wrong." — Name, one-line credential (e.g. "built this exact pipeline for two other regional PM companies")
steps.why: Removing pressure paradoxically increases reply rate: it signals you're not desperate, which itself is a credibility signal.

faded.problem: Now write the equivalent for a different target: a boutique bookkeeping firm (QuickBooks-based) whose owner posted in a Facebook group complaining about spending Sunday nights manually categorising transactions for month-end close.

blanks.prompt: What specific, observed signal do you open with? (one phrase)
blanks.answer: the Sunday night transaction categorising complaint
accept: sunday night categorizing post
the facebook post about categorizing transactions
blanks.why: Same move as the AppFolio hiring post — reference the thing they actually said or did, not a guess about their industry in general.

blanks.prompt: State the mechanism in plain language, one sentence, with a rough before/after number.
blanks.answer: an automated categorisation pipeline that learns their chart of accounts and flags only the uncertain transactions for review, cutting a multi-hour Sunday session to about twenty minutes
accept: automated transaction categorization saving hours
blanks.why: The number has to be plausible and modest enough to be believable on a first message — overpromising here costs credibility even if technically achievable.

blanks.prompt: What's the small, specific, no-call ask?
blanks.answer: offer to run one real month of their transactions through it and send back the categorised result, no call required
accept: send a sample output
offer a free trial run on one month of data
blanks.why: The proof is the ask, not a meeting about the proof. It also gives you a natural second message: sending the actual result.

contentSections.procedure: **Observed signal → plain-language mechanism with a real number → small specific ask → no-pressure close.** Every step is doing something a generic template structurally cannot: proving you looked, proving it works, and lowering the cost of saying yes.

contentSections.body: The observed signal proves you looked. The number proves it works. The small ask lowers the cost of finding out.

contentSections.title: The written version of your positioning

contentSections.body: A one-pager or a pinned LinkedIn post does the same job as the outreach message, at scale, for the people who find you rather than the other way round. Same structure, different delivery: it has to survive a fifteen-second skim from someone who has never heard of you.

contentSections.question: A stranger gives your one-pager four seconds before deciding whether to keep reading. What's the single most common reason a one-pager loses that four seconds?
contentSections.answer: It opens with the consultant's background or philosophy instead of the reader's specific problem — the reader can't yet tell if it's relevant to them, so they stop.
contentSections.hint: Think about what the reader knows in second one, versus what the document assumes they already care about.

contentSections.body: The pattern that survives a skim: **one sentence naming who this is for and the exact process, one before/after that's specific and believable, one piece of proof (even anonymised — lesson four covers this), and one small next step.** Everything else — your background, your methodology, your philosophy about AI — belongs on a second page or a second scroll, not the first four lines. Most one-pagers fail by leading with the consultant's story instead of the reader's problem; the reader doesn't yet care who you are, only whether you've solved this specific thing before.
Lead with the reader's problem, not your story. The story earns its place on line five, after the reader already knows this is for them.

title: Proof when you can't name the client
description: Most of your best work is under NDA or just informally private. You still need proof a stranger can check — here's what's usable without naming anyone.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which forms of proof survive client confidentiality without needing permission
Produce an anonymised case study that still reads as specific and checkable

contentSections.title: What you're actually allowed to show

contentSections.body: Your best engagement to date: you cut a regional insurer's claims-intake time from four days to six hours. You'd love to lead every pitch with that number. Your contract has a confidentiality clause that means naming them, or anything that makes them identifiable, could be a real problem.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding what's safe to put in a public case study about the claims-intake project.
contentSections.question: Which of these can you publish without asking the client first?

items.label: "A regional P&C insurer" and "cut claims-intake time from four days to six hours"
The general shape of the pipeline — OCR, a classification step, human review queue — without proprietary internals
The company's actual name, even just once, "for credibility"
A screenshot of their actual dashboard showing real (if blurred) claim numbers

explanation.aggregate: This is the safe core of a case study: an industry category vague enough to not identify them (there are hundreds of "regional P&C insurers"), plus a real, specific metric. Nothing here identifies the company.
explanation.generic_tools: The architecture pattern — OCR, classify, human-in-the-loop — is your general methodology, reusable and non-proprietary. Describing it teaches a reader something real without exposing anything belonging to the client.
explanation.company_name: Naming them, even once, even 'for credibility,' is exactly what an NDA exists to prevent. It also isn't necessary — the metric does the credibility work; the name adds almost nothing on top of it.
explanation.screenshot: A blurred screenshot of real data is still often identifiable — from a distinctive UI, a partial number, a watermark you missed. Recreate the pattern with obviously fabricated sample data instead; it shows the same mechanism with zero exposure.

contentSections.synthesis: The rule that covers all four: publish the *pattern and the number*, never the *identity or the raw artefact*. A reader evaluating you cares whether the mechanism is real and the outcome is real — not which specific company it happened at.

contentSections.body: This is worth checking against your actual contract language, not just assuming — some clients are fine being named once you ask (a quick "can I reference this project anonymously, no company name, just the industry and the result?" email costs nothing and often gets a yes even where full naming wouldn't). Never publish first and ask forgiveness later; a client who feels exposed after the fact won't refer you, whatever the case study says.
Publish the pattern and the number. Never the identity or the raw artefact — and ask before you assume 'anonymised' is enough.

contentSections.title: Proof that doesn't need a client at all

contentSections.body: Early on, you may not have a finished client engagement to anonymise yet. That's not a dead end — it just means the proof has to come from work you own outright.

contentSections.question: You have zero paid clients yet. Can you still produce proof a stranger would find convincing?
contentSections.answer: Yes — a sandbox build against synthetic data, a public teardown of a real broken process, or a written playbook of your method all require nobody's permission and can be more convincing than a vague testimonial.
contentSections.hint: Proof doesn't require a client. It requires a real, checkable claim — and you can generate that entirely on your own.

contentSections.body:
Three sources of proof that need nobody's permission because you own them completely:

- **A public sandbox build.** Build the exact kind of pipeline you'd sell, against public or synthetic data, and publish it as a working demo or a short teardown video. "Here's a live invoice-matching bot running against sample AppFolio exports" is proof a stranger can click through themselves.
- **A teardown of a public, broken process.** Pick a publicly visible workflow that's obviously manual or clunky (a competitor's public support form, a well-known company's public job posting that reveals a manual process) and publish your own redesign of it. This is analysis, not a client engagement, and it shows judgment.
- **A written playbook or template.** Publish the actual decision framework you use — how you scope a claims-intake automation, say — as a free resource. This proves depth of thinking even with zero client history behind it, and it's often what gets shared into exactly the vertical communities from lesson two.
A sandbox build, a public teardown, or a written playbook are all proof you own outright — useful before you have a single anonymisable client, too.

title: Saying no to work that will hurt you
description: Some engagements cost more than they pay — in scope creep, in unpaid invoices, in reputational damage from something that was doomed before you started. Recognising them before the contract, not after.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a prospective engagement against a fixed set of business-risk red flags
Decline an engagement in a way that preserves the relationship

contentSections.title: The engagement that was always going to go badly

contentSections.body: Six weeks in, a project you took because the fee was good is now four scope changes past the original brief, the client hasn't paid the second invoice, and the person who hired you keeps saying "just one more thing" in a tone that means it never was going to be one more thing. Every one of these signs was visible in the first call.

contentSections.scenario: During the first call, the prospective client says: "We need this done in two weeks, we don't really have a fixed budget yet, and honestly we're not totally sure what 'success' looks like — we'll know it when we see it."
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism that makes this a red flag, not just an inconvenience?

options.label: The timeline is simply too aggressive for good work
Without a defined budget or success criteria, there's no shared basis to ever agree the work is done — scope will expand indefinitely and payment will stay in dispute
It signals the client is disorganised generally and will be annoying to work with

feedback.timeline: A tight timeline alone is a negotiable constraint, not necessarily fatal — you can scope smaller and still deliver something real.
feedback.no_basis: Right. "We'll know it when we see it" means there is no fixed target either of you can point to when the invoice is due. That's not a communication style, it's a structural gap — every deliverable becomes debatable, and every debate favors whoever's holding the money.
feedback.disorganised: True, probably, but 'annoying' undersells the actual mechanism — the real cost here is financial and contractual, not just a difficult personality.

contentSections.mechanism: **No fixed budget plus no fixed success criteria means no fixed endpoint — and an engagement with no endpoint doesn't get harder, it gets indefinite.** This is the pattern to listen for in a first call, not something you discover in week six. The fix, if the relationship is otherwise worth pursuing, is a scoped fixed-price pilot with an explicit definition of done — covered in the contracts phase — not proceeding on a handshake.

contentSections.body:
A short, real checklist worth running mentally on every first call:

- **No fixed budget or success criteria** — covered above.
- **Timeline that's only achievable by skipping the parts that make the work safe** (no testing window, no client review stage).
- **A history of not paying on time, visible from a reference check or even a quick search of public complaints.**
- **The person hiring you isn't the person who can actually approve the scope or the invoice** — you'll be re-selling the same work internally at every stage.
- **They want a specific number promised up front that you can't actually guarantee** ("promise me this cuts headcount by exactly three people") — this one also has an ethical dimension the ethics-practice phase goes into more, but it's a business risk on its own: a promise you can't keep is a dispute waiting to happen.
The red flags are visible on the first call. The cost of ignoring them shows up in week six, not week one.
Declining well matters because the same person often comes back later with a better-scoped project, or refers someone else — a badly handled 'no' costs you both, a well-handled one costs you nothing.

contentSections.title: The client who wants a promise you can't make
contentSections.opening: A prospective client — a mid-size logistics company — wants you to automate their dispatcher scheduling. In the discovery call, the owner says: "I need you to guarantee this cuts our dispatch headcount by two people within sixty days, that's the whole business case for my board."

ask.situation: You know from experience that headcount outcomes depend on decisions the company makes after the tool exists, not on the tool itself — you can build something that makes two dispatchers' jobs faster, but whether that becomes a headcount cut is a management decision you don't control.
ask.question: How do you respond in the moment?

choices.label: Agree to the guarantee — you're confident the tool will be good, and you need the work
choices.consequence: You win the engagement. Sixty days later the tool works well but headcount hasn't changed because the board hadn't actually decided to act on it. The client considers the engagement a failure regardless of the tool's quality.

choices.label: Tell them you can't guarantee headcount outcomes and end the call
choices.consequence: Technically honest, but you've also closed the door on a real opportunity that might still be scopeable — the underlying need is real, only the specific guarantee is the problem.

choices.label: Separate what you can guarantee (the tool's behaviour) from what you can't (the board's decision), and offer to build the business case data alongside the build

response.situation:
You say: "I can guarantee dispatcher time-per-shift drops by a specific, measured amount — I can't guarantee your board decides to reduce headcount off the back of that, since that's an internal call. What I can do is build in the exact reporting that would make that case for you, so the decision is backed by real numbers."

The owner pauses, then says: "Okay — that's actually more useful for the board conversation than a guarantee would've been."
response.question: What's the lesson worth naming here?

choices.label: You didn't lower the ask — you separated the part you control from the part you don't, and offered to serve the part you don't control indirectly
choices.consequence: The engagement proceeds on terms you can actually deliver, with the client's real underlying need — a case for their board — still met.

conceded.summary: The engagement is judged a failure on a metric you never actually controlled.
conceded.lesson: Agreeing to a guarantee you don't control doesn't remove the risk, it just moves it from 'lost this engagement' to 'delivered good work that gets called a failure.' The second is worse for your reputation, not better.

closed.summary: The relationship ends cleanly but a real, fixable opportunity closes with it.
closed.lesson: A flat no protects you from the bad guarantee, but it also throws away the real underlying need — a board case — that you could have served without ever making the guarantee. Declining well means declining the specific bad term, not the whole relationship.

resolved.summary: The client gets what they actually needed, on terms you can actually stand behind.
resolved.lesson: Most bad asks have a real need buried under them. Separating what you control from what you don't, out loud, is usually cheaper than either caving to the ask or walking away from the person making it.

contentSections.body: Decline the specific bad term, not the whole relationship — most bad asks have a real, servable need underneath them.

title: Practice — Rewrite seven weak positioning statements
description: Seven drills applying this module's skills at speed. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the specificity, channel, proof and red-flag rules to unfamiliar statements quickly

contentSections.body: Nothing new. Seven drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting or spread across three — nothing here is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Write your positioning and one proof piece
description: Produce the two documents a real prospective client would actually need to see before saying yes to a call: your positioning statement, and one piece of proof you can show without naming anyone.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a positioning statement that names a specific process and a real market
Produce a piece of proof usable without breaching any confidentiality

contentSections.body: By the end of this lab you'll have two artefacts you can actually use this week: a positioning statement that would survive being read by a stranger in a hurry, and one piece of proof that doesn't require anyone's permission to publish.

contentSections.title: Your positioning statement and proof piece
contentSections.brief: A prospective client — a real or realistic one you could plausibly reach — reads your LinkedIn profile or one-pager for the first time, on their phone, in under fifteen seconds. This lab produces what they'd need to see in that window to keep reading, plus the proof that backs it up.
contentSections.deliverable: A one-sentence positioning statement, a short proof piece (anonymised case study, sandbox description, or playbook excerpt), and the scope wording distinguishing what you've verified from what you haven't.

stages.title: Draft three positioning statements
stages.instructions: Using the two-test rule from lesson one (nameable process, real market size), write three candidate positioning statements from your own actual experience — even small, even unpaid work counts. For each, estimate the market size honestly. Pick the strongest.
stages.checkpoint: You have three real candidates with honest market-size estimates, and you've picked one with a clear reason why.

stages.title: Build the proof piece
stages.instructions: Choose one proof type from lesson four — anonymised case study, sandbox description, teardown, or playbook excerpt — that matches something you've actually done or could genuinely do this week. Write it out in full: the specific number or mechanism, the aggregate (never identifying) framing, and nothing that would expose a real client or company.
stages.checkpoint: The proof piece contains a real, specific claim and no identifying detail — read it back and ask whether a stranger could check it and whether anyone named in it (even implicitly) would object.

stages.title: Combine into a one-pager and self-check
stages.instructions: Using the skim-order from lesson three (who this is for → before/after number → proof → small next step), combine your positioning statement and proof piece into a single short document. Then self-check it against the rubric below.
stages.checkpoint: The full document fits on one page and a stranger reading only the first two lines would know if it's for them.

rubric.criterion: The positioning statement names a specific process, not just an industry
rubric.meets: A reader could say 'that's my exact problem' or 'that's not me' within two seconds.

rubric.criterion: The market behind it is real, not a niche of one
rubric.meets: You could name, roughly, how many companies fit the description — not just the one client you already have.

rubric.criterion: The proof piece contains a real, specific number or mechanism
rubric.meets: Not 'saves time' — an actual before/after figure or a described mechanism a reader could evaluate.

rubric.criterion: Nothing in the proof piece identifies a real client without their consent
rubric.meets: No company name, no verifiable artefact, no detail narrow enough to single out one company.

rubric.criterion: The document follows the skim order
rubric.meets: Who it's for, then the number, then the proof, then a small next step — in that order, on one page.

rubric.criterion: It reads as confident, not apologetic
rubric.meets: No hedging language about being new or unsure — limitations, if stated at all, are stated as scope, not apology.

contentSections.body: A positioning statement without proof is a claim. A proof piece without positioning is unfindable. You need both, on one page, in that order.

title: The clauses that matter in an AI engagement
description: A generic freelance contract template is missing the three or four clauses that actually matter once the deliverable is a pipeline that keeps making decisions after you've been paid and moved on.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which standard-contract clauses need AI-specific rewording
Evaluate a contract draft for the clauses a generic template omits

contentSections.body: You download a standard freelance-services contract template, swap in the client's name, and sign. Eight months later the automation you built starts misclassifying a new category of invoice the client's business grew into, nobody notices for six weeks, and the client asks who's responsible for the bad data that went into their accounting system. The template has a clause about 'deliverables' and nothing about what happens after delivery, because it was written for a logo design, not a system that keeps running.

contentSections.scenario: You're reviewing a generic freelance contract template before sending it to a new client for an invoice-classification automation.
contentSections.question: Which clause is most obviously missing for this kind of work, that wouldn't matter for, say, a one-off website build?

options.label: A payment schedule clause
A clause defining acceptable error/failure rates and what happens when they're exceeded after handover
A clause naming the project title

feedback.payment: Every contract needs this, AI-specific or not — it's not the thing a generic template is missing for this particular kind of work.
feedback.error_rate: Right. A website either works or it doesn't, and once it's live, it does the same thing every time. An automation makes a probabilistic decision on every single invoice, forever, and its error rate will drift as the client's business changes. A generic template has no concept of an ongoing, imperfect decision process — because most of what it's written for isn't one.
feedback.title: This is boilerplate that exists in every template already — not the gap.

contentSections.concept: **A one-off deliverable has a finish line. An automation doesn't — it keeps deciding things after you're paid.** The clauses a generic contract is missing are the ones that answer: what error rate is acceptable, who's watching for drift, and what happens when the system is wrong about something nobody anticipated.

contentSections.body:
Four clauses worth adding to any AI-automation contract that a generic services template usually lacks:

- **Defined acceptable performance** — not "the system will work correctly," but a specific, measurable threshold ("flags for human review any classification below 85% confidence") that both sides agreed to before work started.
- **A monitoring and maintenance boundary** — does your responsibility end at handover, or does it include watching for drift for some defined period? Silence on this defaults to a fight later, not to "obviously not my problem."
- **A human-in-the-loop requirement for consequential decisions** — explicit language that certain decision categories (anything affecting employment, credit, eligibility, pricing to an individual) get routed to a human, not fully automated, regardless of how good the model tests.
- **A change-in-scope trigger tied to data drift** — a clause stating that if the client's underlying data or process changes materially, the original performance guarantee no longer applies until re-validated. Without this, you're implicitly on the hook forever for a system tuned to data that no longer exists.
An automation doesn't have a finish line — the contract needs clauses for what happens after handover, not just what gets delivered.

contentSections.title: Reading a clause for what it actually commits you to

contentSections.body: Contract language is often vague on purpose, from whoever drafted it — vague favors whoever has more leverage to argue about it later. Learning to spot which vague phrase you're about to sign under is a skill, not a legal degree.

contentSections.code:
5.2 Performance
The Contractor shall ensure the Automation performs
accurately and reliably to the Client's satisfaction.

5.3 Support
The Contractor shall provide reasonable ongoing support
as needed.
contentSections.question: What's the single biggest problem with this clause, from your side?

options.label: It doesn't mention a specific software license
"To the Client's satisfaction" and "as needed" are both undefined, open-ended standards you could be held to indefinitely
It should be in a separate document from the main contract

feedback.license: Not the immediate problem — that's a separate, real issue but not what makes this specific clause dangerous.
feedback.undefined: Right. "To the Client's satisfaction" has no measurable definition — it means whatever the client decides it means, whenever a dispute arises. "As needed" has no time boundary or scope limit. Both phrases sound reasonable and are functionally a blank check against your future time.
feedback.location: Document structure isn't the issue here — the substance of the clause is the problem regardless of where it sits.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is replacing subjective standards with measurable ones: "performs accurately" becomes "flags for review any output below X% confidence, measured monthly against a held-out sample"; "reasonable ongoing support as needed" becomes "up to 4 hours per month for the first 90 days post-launch, covering [specific list], billed separately thereafter." Neither rewrite is unfriendly to the client — a client who genuinely wants a functioning system should prefer the measurable version too, since it's the version that's actually enforceable in both directions.

contentSections.body: Any clause using 'as needed,' 'satisfaction,' or 'reasonable efforts' without a measurable definition is a blank check against your future time — rewrite it as a number.

title: Liability when the automation gets something wrong
description: The automation misroutes a claim, miscodes an invoice, or sends a wrong number to a customer. Who's actually on the hook — and what does your contract need to say before that happens, not after?

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish liability exposure you can limit contractually from exposure you can't
Evaluate whether a liability cap in a draft contract is adequate for the engagement's actual risk

contentSections.title: What a liability cap actually does

contentSections.body: An automation you built miscodes a batch of vendor invoices, and the client double-pays three vendors before anyone notices — a real, quantifiable dollar loss, directly traceable to your system. Your contract has no liability clause at all. Without one, in most jurisdictions, you're exposed to the client's actual damages with no ceiling — potentially far more than the fee you were paid.

contentSections.scenario: You add a clause: "Contractor's total liability under this agreement shall not exceed the total fees paid by Client in the preceding twelve months."
contentSections.question: What does this clause actually do, mechanically?

options.label: It eliminates your liability entirely
It caps your financial exposure at a known, bounded number instead of leaving it open to the client's full actual damages
It transfers liability to the client

feedback.eliminates: It doesn't remove liability — you can still be found liable for the capped amount, and in some cases (gross negligence, in many jurisdictions) the cap won't hold at all. It bounds the number, not the fact of liability.
feedback.caps: Right. Without this clause, your exposure is whatever a court decides the client's actual damages were — which could be many multiples of your fee. With it, even if you're found fully liable, the number is capped at something you can actually plan around, typically fees paid.
feedback.transfers: It doesn't move liability onto the client — it limits how much of it can land on you. Nothing here shifts responsibility the other direction.

contentSections.mechanism: **A liability cap doesn't make you not liable — it makes the size of that liability knowable in advance.** This is the single most important clause in any AI-automation contract, because the potential downstream damage from an automated decision (a misrouted claim, a bad price sent to a thousand customers) can be wildly out of proportion to a solo consultant's fee.

contentSections.body: A cap usually carries carve-outs that matter to know about: most caps don't apply to gross negligence, willful misconduct, or breach of confidentiality — and in many places, a court won't enforce a cap against those regardless of what the contract says. This isn't a loophole to close; it's the honest boundary of what a cap can do. It protects you from a genuine mistake in a probabilistic system doing exactly what you both agreed it would do imperfectly — it does not, and shouldn't, protect you from cutting corners you knew were unsafe.
A liability cap bounds the size of your exposure — it doesn't erase it, and it typically doesn't cover gross negligence.

contentSections.title: Sizing the cap to the actual risk

contentSections.body: A cap set at "fees paid" sounds standard because it is standard — but the right number depends on what the automation actually touches. A $4,000 engagement automating internal meeting notes carries a different risk profile than a $4,000 engagement automating pricing sent to live customers.

contentSections.scenario: A consultant built a $6,000 automation that generates draft pricing quotes for a B2B distributor, auto-sent to customers without human review for orders under $500. A pricing bug shipped for eleven days before anyone caught it.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many times the consultant's fee did the resulting damages turn out to be, in a real case with this shape?
contentSections.explanation: Around 9x in this real pattern — underpriced quotes that customers took and the company honored. This is exactly why a flat 'fees paid' cap needs a second look whenever the automation output reaches a customer directly with no human review step: the potential damage scales with what the system touches, not with what you were paid to build it. The fix isn't necessarily a higher cap you can't actually cover — it's often insisting on a human-review gate for anything customer-facing (this connects to the human-in-the-loop clause from lesson one) precisely because that gate is what keeps a small bug from becoming an eleven-day, nine-figure-relative-to-fee incident.

contentSections.body: Practically: for engagements where the automation's output reaches customers, money, or legally consequential decisions without a human review step, either the cap needs to be realistic about the exposure (which usually means it needs to be higher than 'fees paid,' backed by professional liability insurance you actually carry) or the human-review gate needs to be non-negotiable in the design. A solo consultant without insurance generally can't absorb a multiple-of-fee claim regardless of what the contract says — the practical protection is keeping unreviewed automated output away from anything that can generate that kind of damage in the first place.
The right cap size follows what the automation touches, not what you were paid — and for anything unreviewed and customer-facing, a human gate is often cheaper protection than a bigger cap.

title: Data processing terms, in plain language
description: What a client's data actually is, once it's flowing through a third-party API — and the plain-language version of the data-handling terms you need in place before that happens.

learningObjectives.text: Understand what happens to client data once it's sent to a third-party AI API
Identify the data-handling commitments a contract needs before any client data reaches a third party

contentSections.body: You're building a claims-summarisation tool for a regional insurer. The claims contain names, addresses, medical details, sometimes SSNs typed into free-text fields by an adjuster in a hurry. Every one of those fields is about to be sent, as plain text, to a third-party API you don't control the servers for.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding how to handle the SSNs and medical details that occasionally show up in the free-text claim notes before sending them to a third-party LLM API for summarisation.
contentSections.question: What's the right default, before any contract language is even discussed?

options.label: Send it as-is — the API provider's terms of service cover privacy
Strip or mask the specific sensitive fields (SSN patterns, etc.) before the text ever leaves the client's environment, regardless of what any API's terms say
Ask the client to remove sensitive data manually before you start the project

feedback.as_is: An API provider's terms of service govern what *they* do with data once received — they don't reduce the exposure of having sent it there in the first place, and 'the vendor promises to be careful' is not a data-handling plan a client's legal team will accept.
feedback.strip: Right. Pattern-based stripping or masking (SSN formats, common medical-code patterns) before the data leaves the client's own systems is the actual mitigation — it reduces what could ever be exposed, rather than trusting a downstream promise. This is a design decision, not just a contract clause.
feedback.ask_client: Relying on manual removal by a busy adjuster typing quickly is exactly the failure mode that put an SSN in a free-text field in the first place — the fix has to be structural, not a request for more careful behaviour from people who are already not being careful.

contentSections.concept: **Data minimisation is a design decision that happens before it's a contract clause.** The safest data to send to a third party is data that was never sent — stripping, masking, or hashing sensitive fields at the source reduces the actual risk, not just the paperwork around it.

contentSections.body:
In plain language, three things a data processing agreement (DPA) — or the equivalent section in your main contract — needs to say, whether or not you use the term "DPA":

- **Which third parties will process the data, and where.** Name the actual API provider(s). A client is entitled to know their claims data is going to a specific named vendor's servers, not "an AI system."
- **What that vendor does and doesn't do with it** — specifically, whether the vendor trains its models on the data sent through the API. Most major API providers offer an enterprise or API-tier agreement that excludes training by default; the free consumer tier of the same product often does not. This is a real, checkable fact per vendor, not a guess.
- **What happens to the data after the engagement ends** — deletion timelines, whether you (the consultant) retain any copies for debugging or testing, and for how long.
Strip sensitive fields at the source before they ever leave the client's systems — that's a design decision, and it happens before any contract clause matters.

You test a prototype using a free, consumer-facing chat interface because it's fast and familiar. It works. You ship the exact same integration to production. Nobody checked whether that tier's terms allow the provider to use submitted data for model training — a detail that matters enormously for a client's medical or financial data and is easy to miss because the paid API tier of the same company often has completely different terms.

contentSections.code:
Data Processing: Contractor will use industry-standard
AI tools to process Client data as necessary to deliver
the Automation.
contentSections.question: What's missing that a client's legal or compliance team will flag immediately?

options.label: The clause is too short
It doesn't name the specific vendor(s), API tier, or training-data policy — 'industry-standard AI tools' could mean anything, including a consumer tier that trains on submitted data
It should be signed by both parties separately

feedback.short: Length isn't the issue — a precise, short clause naming the actual vendor and tier would be fine. This one is short *and* vague, and it's the vagueness that's the problem.
feedback.vague_vendor: Right. 'Industry-standard AI tools' commits to nothing checkable. A client can't evaluate their actual exposure without knowing which vendor, which tier, and whether that tier trains on submitted data — and neither can you, six months later, when you've forgotten which tier you used for which client.
feedback.signature: Signature process is unrelated to what the clause actually says.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A defensible version names the vendor and product tier explicitly ("Contractor will process Client data using [Vendor]'s API-tier service, which per [Vendor]'s current data usage policy does not use submitted data for model training") and commits to notifying the client before switching vendors or tiers mid-engagement. This is checkable, specific, and protects both sides — the client knows exactly what they agreed to, and you have a paper trail if a vendor's policy changes later.

contentSections.body: Name the actual vendor and API tier in the contract, and confirm the training-data policy yourself — don't assume the paid tier behaves like the free one you prototyped with.

title: IP: who owns the prompts and the pipeline
description: The client owns the outcome. Whether they own your reusable prompt library, your general pipeline architecture, and the code itself is a separate question you need to answer before you build the same thing for your next client.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate an IP clause for whether it accidentally signs away reusable general-purpose components

contentSections.title: The clause that quietly ends your business model

contentSections.body: A standard "work for hire" clause says everything you create during the engagement belongs to the client. You sign it without reading closely. Eighteen months later you've built the same invoice-classification pipeline for four different clients — the general architecture, the prompt templates, the error-handling pattern — and one of the first four clients notices and points out, correctly, that per your own contract, they own all of it.

contentSections.scenario: A generic "work for hire" clause assigns the client ownership of "all work product created during the engagement."
contentSections.question: Why does this clause cause a real problem for a consultant who reuses general architecture across clients — beyond just being 'unfair'?

options.label: It's a formality that doesn't actually get enforced

"All work product" doesn't distinguish between the client-specific configuration (genuinely theirs) and your general-purpose, pre-existing methodology (which you built independently and reuse across clients) — so it can be read to assign both
It only applies to code, not to prompts or architecture

feedback.formality: It's enforceable exactly as written — courts and clients both take 'all work product' language literally, and 'unfair' is not a legal argument once you've signed it.
feedback.no_distinction: Right. Your general pipeline pattern — the reusable architecture, the prompt structures, the error-handling approach — is the actual asset your consulting business is built on. An undifferentiated 'all work product' clause can be read to hand every bit of that to whichever client happens to say so first, which is a mechanism that quietly makes it impossible to reuse your own accumulated expertise.
feedback.code_only: 'Work product' as a legal term typically covers anything created during the engagement, not just code — prompts, documentation, and architecture diagrams are all plausibly included unless the clause says otherwise.

contentSections.mechanism: **The fix is separating the client's specific configuration from your general-purpose methodology, explicitly, in the contract.** Client owns their trained prompts, their specific data pipeline configuration, their integration code for their systems. You retain your general methodology, your reusable templates, your pre-existing tools — with an explicit license granted to the client to use them as embedded in their deliverable, without owning the underlying IP.

contentSections.body:
Concrete language that does this: *"Client owns the specific configuration, trained prompts, and data integrations created for Client's deliverable ('Client Materials'). Contractor retains ownership of its pre-existing methodologies, general-purpose templates, and reusable architecture patterns ('Contractor IP'), and grants Client a perpetual license to use any Contractor IP as embedded in the delivered Automation."*

The client gets everything they need to run and modify their system. You keep the ability to build the same kind of thing for the next client without renegotiating your own accumulated expertise every time.
Separate 'Client Materials' (their specific configuration) from 'Contractor IP' (your reusable methodology) explicitly, or a generic work-for-hire clause can quietly claim both.

A well-tuned system prompt — the one that took you six iterations to get an LLM reliably extracting the right fields from a messy PDF — feels like just text. It's actually one of the most valuable and most reusable artefacts in the whole engagement, and it's exactly the kind of thing an undifferentiated IP clause quietly takes.

contentSections.question: Is a refined prompt template the kind of thing worth explicitly protecting in a contract, or is it too minor to bother with?
contentSections.answer: Worth protecting explicitly — a well-tuned prompt template can represent hours of iteration and is one of the most reusable assets in your whole practice, exactly the kind of thing a generic 'all work product' clause can quietly sign away.
contentSections.hint: Think about how many iterations it took to get that prompt reliable, and how many future clients could benefit from the same underlying structure.

contentSections.body: Treat prompt libraries the same way a software consultant treats an internal framework: something built once, refined across many engagements, licensed into each specific deliverable rather than sold outright each time. Practically, that means keeping your general-purpose prompt templates in your own private repository, and delivering client-specific *configured* versions (with the client's own field names, business rules, and edge cases baked in) as part of the deliverable — the configured version is genuinely theirs; the underlying template structure is genuinely yours, and the contract should say so in exactly those words.
A refined prompt template is a reusable asset like any internal framework — deliver the client-configured version, keep the underlying template.

title: When to get an actual lawyer
description: This module gives you enough to draft a reasonable contract and spot a bad one. It does not make you a lawyer. Knowing exactly where that line sits is itself a professional skill.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate which contract or engagement situations require a licensed lawyer rather than a template

contentSections.title: What this module qualifies you to do, and what it doesn't

contentSections.body: You now know what a liability cap does, why 'as needed' is dangerous, and how to split IP ownership sensibly. None of that makes you qualified to draft a contract for a client in a heavily regulated industry, or to know whether your state's specific case law actually enforces the liability cap you wrote. Those are different, narrower questions, and they're exactly the ones worth paying a lawyer a few hundred dollars to answer once, rather than guessing.

contentSections.scenario: You're about to sign a contract for a new engagement.
contentSections.question: In which of these situations does this module's knowledge genuinely stop being enough, and an actual lawyer becomes worth the cost?

items.label: The client is a healthcare provider and the automation touches data plausibly covered by health-privacy regulation
The contract value is large enough (multi-month, five- or six-figure) that a dispute would be genuinely damaging, not just annoying
The client's own lawyer sends back a heavily redlined version of your contract with unfamiliar terms
A small, first-time engagement with a local business you already know personally, using your own reviewed template

explanation.healthcare: Regulated-industry data-handling requirements (health privacy law, in this example) have specific, jurisdiction-dependent obligations that go well beyond the plain-language data-handling principles in lesson three. Getting this wrong isn't just a business risk, it can be a compliance violation with penalties neither you nor your template anticipated.
explanation.high_value: The cost of an hour of a lawyer's time is trivial against the cost of a genuine dispute on a large engagement. Size of exposure should scale directly with how much you lean on professional review rather than a self-drafted template.
explanation.client_lawyer: Once the other side has a lawyer actively negotiating language, you're no longer in a peer-to-peer conversation about reasonable terms — you're in a legal negotiation, and showing up to that without your own counsel is a structurally weak position regardless of how well you understand contracts generally.
explanation.small_first: This is exactly the situation your own reviewed template is built for — small stakes, known relationship, standard terms. Sending this to a lawyer isn't wrong, but it's not where the real risk in your practice lives, and treating every engagement as needing one erodes the actual judgment this module is trying to build.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern across the first three: regulated data, real financial exposure, and an opposing lawyer are all situations where the cost of being wrong scales past what a template — however well reasoned — can absorb. That's the actual line, not 'anything involving a contract.'

contentSections.body: Practically, this usually means: get your core contract template reviewed once by a lawyer, as a fixed, bounded cost, rather than paying for bespoke review on every engagement. Then use that reviewed template as your default, and pay for one-off legal review specifically when a given engagement crosses one of the four lines above. This keeps legal cost proportional to actual risk instead of either skipping it entirely or treating every contract as a bespoke legal project you can't afford the time or money for.
Get your core template reviewed once, as a fixed cost. Pay for one-off review specifically when regulated data, real financial exposure, or an opposing lawyer is involved.

contentSections.title: A bad-day version of legal diligence

contentSections.body: On a low-capacity day, a full contract review is off the table. A five-minute version isn't: run the four-question checklist below before signing anything, even from bed.

contentSections.question: Put these four quick checks in the order that catches the biggest risk fastest, for a low-energy pre-signature scan.
steps: Does the data involved touch health, financial, or other regulated categories?
Is there a liability cap, and does it look reasonable relative to what the automation touches?
Are 'as needed,' 'satisfaction,' or other undefined standards present anywhere?
Does the IP clause distinguish client-specific configuration from your reusable methodology?
contentSections.explanation: Regulated data first, because it's the one that changes everything else about the engagement — including possibly whether you should take it without a lawyer at all. The liability cap is next because it's the single highest-stakes financial term. Undefined standards and the IP split matter, but a bad version of either usually costs you time or reputation rather than catastrophic exposure — worth catching, but correctly last in a five-minute scan.

contentSections.body: A five-minute, four-question scan from bed still catches the biggest risks — regulated data and the liability cap first.

title: Practice — Flag the dangerous clause in seven contract extracts
description: Seven drills applying this module's skills at speed. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Apply clause-reading, liability, data-handling and IP rules to unfamiliar contract extracts quickly

contentSections.body: Nothing new. Seven drills across the module's skills. Do them in one sitting or spread across three — nothing here is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Assemble your own standard terms
description: Produce the short set of standard contract terms you'll actually reuse across engagements, with a plain-language note on why each clause is there.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a set of standard AI-engagement contract terms covering performance, liability, data and IP
Justify each clause's inclusion in language a client without a legal background could follow

contentSections.body: By the end of this lab you'll have the reusable core of every contract you send from now on — not a full legal document (that still needs the one-time lawyer review from lesson five), but the specific clause language and the reasoning behind each one, so you're never drafting from a blank generic template again.

contentSections.title: Your standard terms
contentSections.brief: You're about to send your third engagement contract this quarter, and you've been rewriting the same clauses from scratch each time, slightly differently, with no consistent standard. This lab produces the reusable set.
contentSections.deliverable: A short (one-to-two page) standard terms document covering performance definition, liability cap, data handling, and IP ownership — each clause paired with a one-sentence plain-language note on why it's there.

stages.title: Draft the performance and liability clauses
stages.instructions: Write a measurable performance-definition clause (not 'works correctly' — a specific, checkable threshold) and a liability-cap clause sized to a plausible real engagement of yours. For the cap, note explicitly what it does and doesn't cover, per lesson two's carve-outs.
stages.checkpoint: Both clauses replace any subjective language with a specific, measurable standard, and the cap states its own limits.

stages.title: Draft the data-handling and IP clauses
stages.instructions: Write a data-processing clause naming a real or plausible specific vendor and API tier and its training-data policy. Then write the Client Materials / Contractor IP split from lesson four, in your own words, specific enough that a client reading it knows exactly what they own versus what you retain.
stages.checkpoint: The data clause names an actual vendor and tier rather than 'industry-standard AI tools,' and the IP clause clearly separates the two categories.

stages.title: Add the plain-language notes and self-check
stages.instructions: For each of the four clauses, add one sentence a non-lawyer client could read and understand why the clause exists — not legal justification, just the plain reason. Then self-check against the rubric below.
stages.checkpoint: A client with no legal background could read the whole document and understand what each clause protects and why.

rubric.criterion: The performance clause is measurable, not subjective
rubric.meets: No phrase like 'works correctly' or 'to Client's satisfaction' survives — replaced with a specific, checkable threshold.

rubric.criterion: The liability cap is sized to a real, plausible engagement and states its own limits
rubric.meets: A number tied to fees or a defined amount, with an honest note that gross negligence typically isn't covered.

rubric.criterion: The data clause names an actual vendor and tier
rubric.meets: Not 'industry-standard AI tools' — a specific, checkable vendor and product tier with a stated training-data policy.

rubric.criterion: The IP clause distinguishes Client Materials from Contractor IP
rubric.meets: A client reading it knows exactly what's theirs to modify freely and what the consultant retains for reuse.

rubric.criterion: Every clause has a plain-language note
rubric.meets: A non-lawyer could read the note and understand why the clause exists, without needing the legal phrasing explained.

rubric.criterion: It fits on one to two pages
rubric.meets: Concise enough to actually get read by a client before signing, not buried in boilerplate.

contentSections.body: A reusable standard-terms document, reviewed once by a lawyer and reused every time, is what turns contract drafting from a recurring risk into a five-minute customisation.

title: Checkpoint — Contracts, Liability and Data
description: Ten questions across this module. Ungraded, untimed — this is the second module of the phase, so all ten pull from here.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions without looking them up

questions.from: This module — Contracts, Liability and Data
questions.prompt: Why does an automation need clauses a one-off deliverable doesn't?

options.label: Automations are always more expensive
An automation keeps making decisions after handover, with no natural finish line
Automations require more code

questions.explanation: A website works the same way every time once live; an automation makes a fresh probabilistic decision on every input, forever, which is why performance thresholds and drift clauses matter.

questions.from: This module — Contracts, Liability and Data
questions.prompt: What's wrong with a clause requiring 'reasonable support as needed'?

options.label: Nothing — it's standard, safe language
It's an undefined, open-ended standard with no measurable threshold or time boundary
It's illegal in most jurisdictions

questions.explanation: Undefined standards like 'as needed' or 'to Client's satisfaction' function as a blank check against your future time — replace them with numbers.

questions.from: This module — Contracts, Liability and Data
questions.prompt: What does a liability cap actually do?

options.label: Eliminates liability entirely
Bounds the size of financial exposure at a known number instead of leaving it open-ended
Transfers liability to the client

questions.explanation: A cap doesn't remove liability — it makes the size of it knowable and plannable, typically tied to fees paid.

questions.from: This module — Contracts, Liability and Data
questions.prompt: What do most liability caps NOT cover, regardless of contract wording?

options.label: Ordinary, good-faith imperfection in a probabilistic system
Gross negligence or willful misconduct
Anything related to data handling

questions.explanation: Most caps carve out gross negligence and willful misconduct, and courts often won't enforce a cap against those even if the contract is silent.

questions.from: This module — Contracts, Liability and Data
questions.prompt: What's the safest default for sensitive fields (like SSNs in free-text notes) before sending data to a third-party API?

options.label: Send as-is and rely on the API vendor's terms of service
Strip or mask sensitive fields before the data ever leaves the client's environment
Ask the client's staff to be more careful

questions.explanation: Data minimisation at the source is a design decision, not just a contract clause — it reduces actual risk rather than trusting a downstream promise.

questions.from: This module — Contracts, Liability and Data
questions.prompt: Why can testing on a free consumer AI tier be misleading before shipping on a paid API tier?

options.label: The free tier is always slower
Free and paid tiers from the same provider are often governed by separate data-training policies
Free tiers don't support the same features

questions.explanation: The mechanism works the same on both tiers, but the data-handling terms — especially whether submitted data trains the model — can differ completely between them.

questions.from: This module — Contracts, Liability and Data
questions.prompt: In the Client Materials / Contractor IP split, what does the consultant retain?

options.label: Everything created during the engagement
General-purpose reusable methodology and templates, licensed to the client as embedded in their deliverable
Nothing — all IP belongs to the client by default

questions.explanation: The consultant retains their pre-existing, reusable methodology (Contractor IP); the client owns their specific configuration (Client Materials).

questions.from: This module — Contracts, Liability and Data
questions.prompt: Which of these situations most clearly warrants paying for one-off legal review beyond a standard reviewed template?

options.label: A small, known local client using standard terms
A large contract involving regulated health data and the client's own legal team
Any engagement mentioning AI at all

questions.explanation: Regulated data, high financial exposure, and an opposing lawyer are the lines from lesson five where the cost of being wrong exceeds what a template can absorb.

questions.from: This module — Contracts, Liability and Data
questions.prompt: What's the recommended practical approach to legal cost across a practice?

options.label: Never involve a lawyer — it's too expensive for a solo practice
Get a core template reviewed once as a fixed cost, then pay for one-off review only when specific risk lines are crossed
Have every single contract fully reviewed by a lawyer before signing

questions.explanation: This keeps legal cost proportional to actual risk, rather than either skipping legal review entirely or treating every contract as a bespoke legal project.

questions.from: This module — Contracts, Liability and Data
questions.prompt: In the five-minute bad-day contract scan, which check should come first?

options.label: Whether the IP clause is present
Whether the data involved touches a regulated category
Whether the font size is readable

questions.explanation: Regulated data changes everything else about the engagement's risk profile, including possibly whether to take it without a lawyer at all — so it's checked first.
