title: What actually changes, and how often
description: The feeling that everything in AI changes weekly is mostly a feeling. Separating what actually changes at a pace that matters to a working consultant from what just generates a lot of noise about changing.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish the layers of an AI-consulting practice that change quickly from those that change slowly

contentSections.body: A new model release, a new framework, a new "AI agent" product launch — there's genuinely something new to read about most days. A consultant who tries to track all of it at the same level of attention burns their entire available learning budget on things that mostly don't change what they'd actually recommend a client do.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding how much attention to give three different kinds of AI news: a new foundation model release with better benchmark scores, a new no-code automation platform launching, and a well-known API provider changing its pricing tiers.
contentSections.question: Which of these three actually changes what you'd recommend to a typical client, most of the time?

options.label: The new model release — better benchmarks always change the recommendation

None of them reliably, on their own — the underlying problem-solving approach (data quality, human-in-the-loop design, proportionate scope) barely moves; what moves faster is cost and access, worth a lighter, ongoing scan rather than deep tracking of every release
The new automation platform — new tools always obsolete the old approach

feedback.model: A benchmark improvement rarely changes the actual engagement approach — the scoping method, the human-review gates, the data-handling discipline from earlier modules are unaffected by which specific model does the underlying text generation. Benchmarks move fast; recommendations mostly don't.
feedback.neither_reliably: Right. The layer that changes fast — specific model capabilities, tool launches, pricing — mostly swaps out an interchangeable component underneath a much more stable layer: how you scope, how you handle data, when you insist on human review. Tracking the fast layer closely is usually lower-value than it feels; a periodic lighter scan (this module's actual method) captures what matters without the daily anxiety of trying to keep up with everything.
feedback.platform: New platforms launch constantly and most don't actually change the underlying professional judgment calls this whole course has been teaching — they're new implementation options, not new principles.

contentSections.concept: **Three layers move at three different speeds: principles (scoping, human-in-the-loop, data handling) change slowly; capability and cost (what a given model or tool can actually do, and what it costs) change faster; specific product names and marketing change constantly and mostly don't matter.** Most of the anxiety about "falling behind" comes from tracking the fastest, least consequential layer.

contentSections.body: This doesn't mean capability and cost changes don't matter — they genuinely do, and ignoring them means quoting a client a workaround for a limitation that got fixed six months ago, or missing that a task that used to need a custom pipeline is now a five-minute off-the-shelf job. It means the right amount of attention is a periodic, bounded check specifically on capability and cost, not a constant, anxious scan of everything being announced, most of which is marketing noise about the fastest-moving and least consequential layer.
Principles change slowly, capability and cost change at a moderate pace worth a periodic check, and daily product news is mostly noise not worth tracking closely.

contentSections.title: A bad-day version of the question

contentSections.body: On a low-energy day, "staying current" can feel like an impossible, open-ended obligation. It isn't, once it's reframed as a bounded, periodic question rather than a constant one.

contentSections.question: Does 'staying current' in this field require daily attention to keep from falling meaningfully behind?
contentSections.answer: No — because the layer that changes daily (specific releases and marketing) mostly doesn't change your actual recommendations. A periodic, bounded check on capability and cost is enough to stay genuinely current, without daily tracking.
contentSections.hint: Reconnect this to the three-layer distinction from pod one — which layer would daily tracking actually be following?

contentSections.body: The reframe that matters here: "staying current" isn't a race you're always slightly losing, it's a bounded, periodic task — a fixed amount of time, on a fixed cadence, checking a specific, narrow thing (capability and cost changes relevant to your niche), not an open-ended obligation to know everything happening in AI. The next four lessons build exactly that bounded system.
Staying current is a bounded, periodic task, not an open-ended race — that reframe alone removes most of the anxiety attached to it.

title: Sources worth reading and the noise to drop
description: A curated, small set of sources checked on a fixed cadence beats a large, unbounded feed you feel guilty about not keeping up with.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate an information source for whether it reliably surfaces capability/cost changes relevant to your niche

contentSections.title: Why more sources make you less current, not more

contentSections.body: Following forty AI-focused accounts, three newsletters, and a handful of subreddits feels thorough. In practice it produces a feed dominated by whoever posts most often and most dramatically — which correlates poorly with whoever is actually reporting something that changes what you'd tell a client.

contentSections.scenario: Two consultants each spend roughly the same 30 minutes a week on staying current. One follows a broad, large set of general AI accounts and skims whatever's trending. The other reads three specific sources: the official release notes/changelog for the two or three vendors their niche actually depends on, one vertical-specific community (per module one's channel-finding lesson) where practitioners discuss what's actually changed for them, and one curated weekly digest from a source with a track record of accuracy over hype.
contentSections.question: Why does the second consultant end up more genuinely current, despite reading less volume?

options.label: The second consultant is simply a faster reader

A broad general feed is dominated by volume and hype, which is a poor proxy for relevance to your specific niche; a small, targeted set of sources filters for exactly what would change a recommendation
Official changelogs are always more accurate than community sources

feedback.speed: Reading speed isn't the variable here — both consultants spend the same 30 minutes.
feedback.signal: Right. Volume in a broad feed is driven by what generates engagement, which is a bad proxy for what's actually consequential to a specific practice. A small set of sources chosen specifically for relevance to your niche filters for signal directly, rather than filtering hype after the fact from a much larger pile.
feedback.changelogs_only: Changelogs matter but aren't sufficient alone — the vertical community catches practical, real-world implications a changelog entry doesn't spell out, like a capability change that quietly breaks a common workaround.

contentSections.mechanism: **A small, deliberately chosen set of sources beats a large, unbounded one — not because it's faster to read, but because it's chosen to filter for relevance rather than for volume.** The three-source pattern (vendor changelogs for your specific stack, one vertical community, one curated accuracy-focused digest) is a reasonable default; the specific sources should match your actual niche, not a generic 'AI news' list.

contentSections.body: A quick test for whether a source belongs in your bounded set: over the last three months, has it surfaced something that actually changed a recommendation you'd give a client, or has it mostly surfaced things that were interesting but changed nothing? A source that's consistently interesting-but-inconsequential is exactly the kind of noise this lesson is about dropping, even if it feels informative to read.
A small set of sources chosen for relevance to your specific niche beats a large, broad feed chosen for volume — test each source by whether it's actually changed a recommendation recently.

The specific three sources are yours to choose, but the categories are worth keeping consistent: something authoritative about your specific tools, something practitioner-level about your specific vertical, and something curated for accuracy over hype at the broader industry level.

contentSections.question: If you had to cut your current information sources down to exactly three, which category would be hardest to justify keeping?
contentSections.answer: For most people it's the broad, general 'AI news' feed — the one that produces the most volume and the least relevance to a specific niche. The vendor changelog and vertical community categories are usually easier to defend, because they're chosen for direct relevance rather than general interest.
contentSections.hint: Ask which category filters by volume rather than by relevance to your specific practice.

contentSections.body: Practically: write down the two or three vendors your practice actually depends on and subscribe to their changelog or release-notes feed directly (not a third-party summary of it). Identify one vertical-specific community from the channel work in module one and check it on the same cadence. Pick one broader industry digest — ideally one with a track record you can check, not just one with a big following — and treat everything outside those three as optional, opportunistic reading rather than an obligation.
Vendor changelogs for your actual stack, one vertical community, one accuracy-focused digest — everything else is optional, not an obligation.

title: Testing a new capability in an hour
description: Reading that a capability changed isn't the same as knowing whether it actually solves a problem you've hit before. A bounded, one-hour test protocol turns a headline into an actual answer.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a bounded, time-limited protocol for testing whether a new capability actually resolves a known past limitation

contentSections.body: A vendor's changelog says a new model version "significantly improves structured data extraction from scanned documents." That sentence alone doesn't tell you whether it actually fixes the specific failure you hit eight months ago on a client's handwritten intake forms. Only a real test does, and the test doesn't need to take more than an hour.

contentSections.question: Put these four steps of a bounded capability test in the order that keeps it actually bounded to about an hour.
steps: Pull the specific real example that failed before — the actual document, prompt, or edge case, not a generic test
Run it against the new capability exactly as the earlier failed attempt was run, changing nothing else
Compare the specific output against the specific old failure, not against a general impression
Write one sentence: does this change what you'd recommend for this specific class of problem, yes or no
contentSections.explanation: Starting from the actual past failure (not a generic test case) is what keeps this bounded and meaningful — you already know exactly what "better" would need to look like. Changing nothing else in the test isolates whether the capability itself improved, rather than conflating it with a different prompt or setup. Comparing specifically rather than generally prevents "huh, seems better" impressions that don't actually answer whether it fixes the known problem. Writing the one-sentence verdict is what turns an hour of testing into something reusable later, instead of a vague memory of having tried it once.

contentSections.body: The discipline that keeps this to an hour rather than a rabbit hole: test against exactly one known past failure, not a broad exploration of "what else can this do now." A broad exploration is genuinely interesting and also genuinely unbounded — there's no natural stopping point. A test against one specific known failure has a built-in stopping point: you either fixed that specific thing or you didn't, and you write the sentence and move on.
Test against one specific known past failure, not a broad exploration — that's what gives the hour a natural stopping point.

contentSections.title: Keeping a running list of test candidates

contentSections.body: The bounded test only works if you have a ready list of past failures worth re-testing, rather than trying to remember one on the spot when a relevant announcement shows up.

contentSections.question: Should you decide what to test the moment you see a relevant announcement, or before?
contentSections.answer: Before — keep a running, short list of past limitations worth re-testing (three to five items is plenty), so when a relevant announcement appears you can immediately match it to a specific candidate rather than inventing a test case on the spot.
contentSections.hint: Think about how much slower and vaguer testing becomes when the test case has to be invented in the moment.

contentSections.body: Practically: keep a short, running list (three to five entries is plenty) of specific past limitations you've hit — the handwritten-form extraction failure, a model's tendency to hallucinate a specific kind of field, a latency problem that made a particular real-time use case infeasible. When a changelog entry or vendor announcement plausibly touches one of these, that's the trigger for the one-hour test from pod one. This turns "staying current" from a vague ongoing feeling into a specific, checkable, bounded action with a clear trigger and a clear stopping point.
Keep a running list of three to five specific past failures. A relevant announcement is the trigger; the one-hour test against that specific item is the response.

title: Updating advice you already gave a client
description: A capability change that fixes a limitation you designed around six months ago creates an obligation most consultants quietly avoid: telling a past client their current system is no longer the best available answer.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate when a capability change is significant enough to warrant proactively contacting a past client
Produce a message that updates prior advice honestly without undermining trust in the original recommendation

contentSections.body: Eight months ago you told a client their document-extraction task needed a human review step for handwritten forms because the model at the time was unreliable on handwriting. You tested a new model version last week using the one-hour protocol from lesson three, and it's now genuinely reliable on that exact case. Telling them means admitting the recommendation you charged for has a shelf life. Not telling them means their process stays needlessly slower than it has to be, indefinitely.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding whether a specific capability change is significant enough to proactively contact a past client about.
contentSections.question: Which of these make proactive contact worth the (mildly awkward) conversation?

items.label: The change would materially reduce their ongoing operating cost or time spent, not just a marginal improvement
It removes a step (like a human review gate) that was specifically load-bearing in your original recommendation, verified against the actual known limitation, not a general capability claim
Any capability change even loosely related to their engagement, to demonstrate ongoing value
A vendor's marketing claim about improvement, without having run the one-hour test from lesson three yourself

explanation.material_cost: A genuinely material improvement in cost or time is worth the conversation — it's real, actionable value for the client, and it's the kind of update a good advisor is expected to flag.
explanation.removes_step: This is exactly the case that matters most: your original advice included a specific safeguard for a specific reason, and that reason no longer holds, verified by your own test rather than a marketing claim.
explanation.any_change: Reaching out about every loosely-related change reads as noise, not value — it also risks the opposite of the goal, training the client to tune out your updates.
explanation.unverified: Contacting a client based on an unverified vendor claim, before running your own test, risks recommending a change that doesn't actually hold up — this is precisely why lesson three's bounded test exists before this step, not instead of it.

contentSections.synthesis: The bar for proactive contact: a change you've personally verified (not just read about) that materially affects cost, time, or a specific safeguard your original advice depended on. Below that bar, it's not worth the interruption; above it, it's part of the job, not an optional extra.

contentSections.body: This connects to the contracts module's monitoring-and-maintenance boundary — if your contract specifies a defined period of responsibility for drift and updates, this kind of proactive contact is arguably already inside scope for that period. Outside any contracted period, it's a relationship-maintenance choice, not an obligation, but it's usually a good one: it's exactly the kind of thing that generates the referral and repeat-business channel from the positioning module.
The bar for proactive contact: a change you've personally verified that materially affects cost, time, or a safeguard your original advice specifically depended on.

contentSections.title: Delivering the update without undermining trust

contentSections.body: "I was wrong before" is not the right framing, and it's also not accurate — the original recommendation was correct given what was true at the time. The framing that's both honest and doesn't erode the client's confidence in your judgment is different.

contentSections.question: What's the difference between "I was wrong before" and the framing this lesson recommends?
contentSections.answer: "I was wrong" implies the original judgment was flawed. The accurate framing is that the recommendation was correct given what was true at the time, and the underlying capability has since changed — the judgment process worked, the input to it changed.
contentSections.hint: The original advice was a correct read of the situation as it existed then. What changed is the situation, not the judgment.

contentSections.body: A template that gets this right: *"When we built [system] eight months ago, [specific limitation] meant a human review step was the right call — I tested this properly last week and that's no longer the case, so it's worth revisiting whether that step still needs to be there. Happy to walk through what would change and what it'd take."* This states plainly that the original call was correct for its time, names the specific thing that changed, and offers a next step — without ever implying the original recommendation was a mistake, because it wasn't.
Frame it as "correct then, the situation changed," never "I was wrong" — because the original judgment was accurate for what was true when you made it.

title: A quarterly review of your own assumptions
description: The bounded weekly and per-announcement habits from this module still leave one gap: the assumption you never revisit because nothing specifically prompted you to. A quarterly review closes that gap on a fixed, low schedule.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a structured quarterly review naming outdated assumptions and the specific advice they affect

contentSections.title: The gap the weekly habit doesn't cover

contentSections.body: The three-source weekly check and the trigger-based one-hour test both depend on something prompting you — an announcement, a changelog entry. Some assumptions go stale without ever being prompted: a belief about what clients in your niche typically need, a default you set once and never questioned, a limitation you assumed was permanent because you never had a reason to re-test it.

contentSections.question: Why can't the weekly source-check and one-hour test habits from earlier lessons catch every outdated assumption on their own?
contentSections.answer: Both are reactive — triggered by an announcement or changelog entry. An assumption nobody announced changing (a belief about typical client needs, a default nobody ever challenged) can go stale silently, with no external trigger to prompt re-examining it.
contentSections.hint: Both earlier habits need something external to prompt them. What happens to an assumption that never gets an external prompt?

contentSections.body: A quarterly review is the deliberately scheduled counterpart to those reactive habits — instead of waiting for a trigger, you set aside a fixed, bounded time (roughly an hour, matching the badDayPath scale of this module) every quarter to ask a specific small set of questions: what did I assume about my niche's needs three months ago that a recent engagement proved wrong or incomplete? What's a default I've been recommending without re-checking whether it's still the best option? What's a past client conversation I should revisit given what's changed since?
A quarterly review is scheduled, not triggered — it's the only habit in this module that catches an assumption nobody ever announced changing.

contentSections.title: Doing the review on a bad day

contentSections.body: A quarterly review sounds like it needs a clear head and a full afternoon. The version that actually happens four times a year is much smaller than that — closer to three written questions than a strategic retreat.

contentSections.problem: Run a real quarterly review for a consultant whose practice centers on invoice-processing automation for property management companies, three months after their last review.

steps.label: What did I assume that a recent engagement proved wrong or incomplete?
steps.work: "I assumed most property management clients wanted full automation of the reconciliation step. My last two clients both specifically wanted a human-review layer even after seeing the automated version work reliably — trust in the number mattered more to them than speed."
steps.why: This is a real, specific correction from lived engagement experience, not a hypothetical — exactly the kind of thing that doesn't show up in a changelog or vendor announcement.

steps.label: What's a default I've been recommending without re-checking?
steps.work: "I've been defaulting to a specific OCR step for scanned invoices without re-testing whether a newer, cheaper option now handles the same accuracy — I haven't run the lesson-three test on this in over three months."
steps.why: This surfaces a candidate for the one-hour test from lesson three — the quarterly review's job here isn't to answer the question, it's to notice the question hasn't been asked in a while.

steps.label: What past client conversation should I revisit?
steps.work: "The client from eight months ago with the handwritten-form limitation — worth checking whether the capability update from lesson four's example applies to them specifically."
steps.why: This connects the quarterly review directly to the proactive-update habit from lesson four, giving it a scheduled prompt rather than relying only on remembering.

faded.problem: Run the same three-question review for a consultant whose practice centers on customer-support ticket triage for DTC e-commerce brands.

blanks.prompt: Name a plausible assumption a recent engagement might have proven wrong or incomplete. (one sentence)
blanks.answer: assumed clients wanted full auto-response for common questions, but a recent client wanted every auto-response reviewed before sending during their first month, to build trust in the system
accept: clients wanted a trial period with human review before full automation
blanks.why: This mirrors the property-management example's shape: a belief about what clients generally want, corrected by a specific, real engagement detail.

blanks.prompt: Name a plausible default worth re-checking against a newer option. (one sentence)
blanks.answer: the specific sentiment-classification approach used for escalation routing hasn't been re-tested against a newer, more accurate option in several months
accept: a routing or classification method that hasn't been re-tested recently
blanks.why: This is a capability/cost-layer candidate for the one-hour test — the review's job is surfacing it, not resolving it on the spot.

blanks.prompt: Name a plausible past client conversation worth revisiting. (one sentence)
blanks.answer: a client from early in the practice who was told multilingual support wasn't feasible within budget at the time, worth checking against current capability and cost
accept: an old client told something wasn't feasible, worth rechecking now
blanks.why: This connects back to lesson four's proactive-update pattern, scheduled rather than left to memory.

contentSections.procedure: **What did a real engagement correct? What default hasn't been re-checked? Which past client conversation deserves revisiting?** Three questions, roughly an hour, four times a year — small enough to survive a low-capacity quarter and still catch what the reactive habits from earlier lessons structurally can't.

contentSections.body: Three questions, about an hour, four times a year — small enough to actually happen, and it's the only habit that catches an assumption nothing external ever prompted you to question.

title: Lab — Run one quarterly capability review
description: Actually run the quarterly review from lesson five, on your own practice, producing a real document naming what changed, what you tested, and which of your advice it revises.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a completed quarterly capability review naming specific changes and their effect on prior advice

contentSections.body: This lab is the actual thing, not a simulation of it — by the end, you'll have run a real quarterly review and produced the document you'd file away and refer back to next quarter, with the sourcing, testing, and review habits from this whole module built into one artefact.

contentSections.title: Your quarterly capability review
contentSections.brief: Treat this as your actual first quarterly review, whether your practice is real, in progress, or still hypothetical — the structure works the same either way, and having a completed first one makes the next three easier.
contentSections.deliverable: A written quarterly review: your three-source list with a recent example of each earning its place, one completed one-hour capability test against a real or plausible past limitation, and the three-question assumption review from lesson five.

stages.title: Confirm your three-source list and one test candidate
stages.instructions: Using lesson two, write your actual three sources (vendor changelog, vertical community, industry digest) with a specific recent example of each passing the relevance test. Then, using lesson three, name one specific past limitation from your running list and state what a genuinely achievable one-hour test against it would look like.
stages.checkpoint: All three sources have a specific, recent, real justification — not just a general reputation — and the test candidate is a specific past failure, not a general capability question.

stages.title: Run the bounded test and the proactive-contact check
stages.instructions: Actually run (or, if no real tool access, walk through in detail exactly how you'd run) the one-hour test from lesson three against your named candidate. Write the one-sentence verdict. Then check the result against lesson four's bar for proactive client contact, and if it clears the bar, draft the update message using the correct framing.
stages.checkpoint: There's a specific, checkable verdict sentence, and a clear decision (with reasoning) on whether it clears the bar for contacting a past client.

stages.title: Complete the three-question assumption review
stages.instructions: Using lesson five's structure, answer the three questions for your own practice: what did a recent engagement correct, what default hasn't been re-checked, and which past client conversation deserves revisiting. Then self-check the whole document against the rubric below.
stages.checkpoint: All three answers are specific and checkable, not general statements about wanting to stay current.

rubric.criterion: The three-source list has a specific, recent justification for each source
rubric.meets: Not general reputation — a specific instance of each source actually changing a recommendation.

rubric.criterion: The capability test targets one specific known past failure
rubric.meets: Not a general capability question — the exact past limitation, named specifically.

rubric.criterion: The test produces a checkable one-sentence verdict
rubric.meets: A clear yes/no on whether this changes a recommendation, not a vague impression.

rubric.criterion: The proactive-contact decision is checked against the actual bar
rubric.meets: Explicitly reasoned against lesson four's criteria, not just a gut call.

rubric.criterion: The three assumption-review answers are specific and checkable
rubric.meets: Concrete enough to act on, not general statements like 'stay current.'

rubric.criterion: The whole document is short enough to actually redo next quarter
rubric.meets: Structured so the same format could be filled in again in roughly an hour, three months from now.

contentSections.body: This document is reusable — the same structure, filled in again in about an hour, is the whole system for staying current without drowning, four times a year.

title: Checkpoint — Staying Current Without Drowning

questions.from: This module — Staying Current Without Drowning
questions.prompt: Per the three-layer model, which layer changes slowly and doesn't move much even with a much better model?

options.label: Principles — like when a human should be the final decision-maker
Product names and marketing
Specific benchmark scores

questions.explanation: Professional principles like human-in-the-loop requirements barely move regardless of which model does the underlying work.

questions.from: This module — Staying Current Without Drowning
questions.prompt: What's the actual test for whether an information source belongs in your bounded set?

options.label: Its follower count
Whether it's recently surfaced something that changed an actual recommendation
How often it posts

questions.explanation: Volume-based measures correlate poorly with relevance; the concrete test is whether the source has actually changed a real recommendation recently.

questions.from: This module — Staying Current Without Drowning
questions.prompt: What keeps a capability test bounded to about an hour?

options.label: Testing against one specific known past failure, which has a built-in stopping point
Using only free tools
Testing every new feature at once

questions.explanation: A specific known failure has a clear yes/no stopping point; a broad exploration of new capability has no natural end.

questions.from: This module — Staying Current Without Drowning
questions.prompt: What gap does the quarterly review close that the reactive weekly habits can't?

options.label: Assumptions that went stale with no external trigger to prompt re-examining them
Errors in the vendor changelogs
The need to test any new capability at all

questions.explanation: The weekly habits are reactive, needing an announcement or changelog as a trigger — a scheduled review is the only habit that catches an untriggered stale assumption.

questions.from: Previous module — Engagements That Survive a Missed Week
questions.prompt: What makes a timeline buffer actually survive to protect a bad week?

options.label: Making it as large as possible
Making it a visible, separately-labeled line item, not folded into the estimate
Telling the client about it verbally

questions.explanation: A buffer with no separate existence gets silently absorbed by optimism; a visible line requires a deliberate decision to spend.

questions.from: Previous module — Engagements That Survive a Missed Week
questions.prompt: What three things does a client-facing incapacity message need to include?

options.label: A full medical explanation
Revised timeline, anything needing their attention now, and when they'll hear next
A promise it won't happen again

questions.explanation: These three give the client what they need to plan; the rest is optional personal disclosure.

questions.from: Previous module — Engagements That Survive a Missed Week
questions.prompt: Why should an async-first structure be stated in the original proposal rather than introduced later?

options.label: It's legally required
The same content reads as a deliberate method up front, and as a reaction or excuse when introduced after a missed commitment
Clients prefer longer proposals

questions.explanation: Timing changes the signal even when the wording is identical — say it before anything's been missed.

questions.from: Previous module — Engagements That Survive a Missed Week
questions.prompt: What's the honest, sufficient case for fixed-fee pricing to a client, without disclosing personal reasons?

options.label: It's simpler to invoice
It gives the client budget certainty — their cost doesn't grow if a stage takes longer for reasons on your side
It's the industry standard

questions.explanation: This framing is true, complete, and centers the client's benefit rather than requiring any personal disclosure.

questions.from: Older module — The Work You Won't Take
questions.prompt: What's the direct test for whether a client wants genuine advice or cover?

options.label: Asking how much they're willing to pay
Asking directly whether a mixed or negative finding would still be useful to them
Checking their industry reputation

questions.explanation: A genuine advisory client says yes; a client seeking cover hesitates or asks for a guaranteed positive outcome.

questions.from: Older module — Contracts, Liability and Data
questions.prompt: What does a liability cap actually do?

options.label: Eliminates liability entirely
Bounds the size of financial exposure at a known number
Transfers liability to the client

questions.explanation: A cap doesn't remove liability — it makes the size of it knowable and plannable.
